scenarios.title: Taking Orders Online for Thali Junction
scenarios.background: Thali Junction is a fictional chain of six vegetarian restaurants in the city of Kesarpur. It is replacing phone orders with a web ordering page: a React single-page app talks to an Express (Node.js) API, which stores orders in PostgreSQL. About 600 orders arrive each day, peaking at 90 in the lunch hour. Each order has a customer, an outlet, a list of dishes with quantities between 1 and 20, and a pickup time. Two junior developers are building the first version in four weeks.
constraints: Orders must never be saved with invalid quantities or pickup times
The same API will later serve a mobile app
Two junior developers have a four-week deadline

questions.prompt: A customer taps 'Place order'. Which request should the React app send to create the order?

options.text: GET /orders/new with every order field in the query string
POST /orders, answered with 201 Created and the new order
PUT /orders, answered with 200 OK and the full order list
PATCH /orders/latest, answered with 204 and an empty body

questions.explanation: Creating a new resource whose id the server assigns is the job of POST on the collection. 201 Created tells the client that a resource was made, and returning the saved order gives the app its id and pickup time to show.

why_others_wrong.a: GET is meant to be safe and must not change data; browsers, proxies and crawlers may repeat or prefetch it, and query strings end up in logs.
why_others_wrong.c: PUT replaces the resource at a URL the client already knows, and returning every order would leak other customers' data.
why_others_wrong.d: PATCH partially updates an existing resource; 'latest' is not a stable address, and it gives no way to create a new order.

questions.key_justification: Creating a resource with a server-assigned id is a POST to the collection, answered with 201 Created.

questions.prompt: The API receives an order with a quantity of -2. What should it respond with?

options.text: 500 Internal Server Error, since saving the row would fail
200 OK, with an error flag set inside the JSON response
401 Unauthorized, since the customer may not order that
400 Bad Request, with a message naming the invalid field

questions.explanation: The problem is in the client's input, so it calls for a 4xx status, and 400 Bad Request is the general code for an invalid request. Naming the field lets the app show the customer exactly what to fix.

why_others_wrong.a: 5xx codes mean the server failed; here the request itself was wrong, and calling it a server error hides that from the client and fills error dashboards.
why_others_wrong.b: A 200 status tells clients, monitoring and retry logic that the request worked, so failures are easy to miss.
why_others_wrong.c: 401 means the request lacks valid authentication; the customer's identity is not the problem here.

questions.key_justification: Invalid client input gets a 4xx status, and 400 Bad Request is the general one.

questions.prompt: The React form already blocks negative quantities. Which two reasons explain why the Express API must still validate every order?

options.text: Anyone can call the API directly with a script or curl, skipping the form entirely
The planned mobile app, or an old cached copy of the web app, may lack the same checks
Browser checks slow the form down, so they should be removed once the API validates
Express refuses requests from non-React clients unless validation code is present
Server-side checks stop HTML attributes such as min and required from working

questions.explanation: The API is the one place every request must pass through, so it is the only place where a rule can be enforced. Client-side checks improve the experience, but they can be skipped by direct calls or be missing from other clients.

why_others_wrong.c: Client checks give instant feedback and save a round trip; they should stay alongside server validation.
why_others_wrong.d: Express accepts any well-formed HTTP request and has no idea which kind of client sent it.
why_others_wrong.e: HTML validation attributes run in the browser and are unaffected by anything the server does.

questions.key_justification: Client validation is for user experience; server validation is the enforcement point.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in order, from the customer's tap on 'Place order' to the confirmation appearing on screen.

options.text: The browser sends the POST request with the order as JSON
The click handler reads the form state and calls fetch()
The Express route validates the body and inserts the order row
The API replies 201 Created with the saved order as JSON
React stores the response in state and shows the confirmation

questions.explanation: The handler builds the request from component state, the browser sends it, and the server validates and saves the order before replying. React can show the confirmation only after the response arrives, because the order id comes from the database.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Showing the confirmation before the API replies, which tells the customer the order succeeded even when validation or the database insert later fails.

questions.key_justification: A client can confirm a server-side action only after the server's response arrives.

scenarios.title: Designing ShikshaSetu's Tutoring Marketplace
scenarios.background: ShikshaSetu is a fictional startup in Nandgiri that connects school students with home tutors for maths and science. Students browse tutor profiles, book one-hour slots and pay in advance; tutors manage their calendar from a dashboard behind a login. The team expects 3,000 tutors and 40,000 students in the first year. Most students find tutors through Google searches such as 'physics tutor Nandgiri', and many browse on low-cost phones over slow mobile data. In the pilot, bookings lived in a shared spreadsheet, and two students booking the same slot at the same moment led to several refunds.
constraints: A tutor slot must never be sold to two students
Public tutor profiles must be indexable by search engines
Login sessions must resist theft through injected scripts
Passwords must stay safe even if the database is leaked

questions.prompt: Where should ShikshaSetu store tutors, students, slots and bookings?

options.text: A JSON file on the API server, rewritten on every new booking
Each browser's localStorage, synced to the server every night
A relational database with a unique constraint on tutor and slot
An in-memory cache only, rebuilt from tutor calendars on restart

questions.explanation: The data is relational (tutors have slots, students have bookings, bookings have payments), and the key rule is that a slot is sold once. A unique constraint on tutor and slot start makes the database reject the second booking even when two requests arrive at the same instant.

why_others_wrong.a: Concurrent requests can overwrite each other's changes to one file, and a file cannot enforce uniqueness or be shared by a second server.
why_others_wrong.b: Each device sees only its own copy, so two students could book the same slot long before any sync runs.
why_others_wrong.d: Memory is lost on restart and is not shared across servers, so bookings would vanish.

questions.key_justification: Enforce a must-never-happen rule with a database constraint, not with application timing.

questions.prompt: After login, where should the web app keep the session so that injected scripts cannot read it?

options.text: In localStorage, so any script on the page can add it as a header
In a URL query parameter appended to every API request it makes
In a global JavaScript variable written into the page on load
In a cookie marked HttpOnly and Secure, with SameSite set

questions.explanation: An HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by JavaScript, so a cross-site scripting bug cannot simply copy the session out. Secure keeps the cookie off plain HTTP, and SameSite limits it being sent on requests started by other sites.

why_others_wrong.a: Anything in localStorage is readable by every script on the page, including an injected one.
why_others_wrong.b: URLs are kept in browser history, server logs and Referer headers, which leaks the session widely.
why_others_wrong.c: A global variable is readable by any script on the page, the same weakness as localStorage.

questions.key_justification: HttpOnly cookies keep session tokens out of reach of page scripts.

questions.prompt: How should the public tutor profiles and the logged-in tutor dashboard be rendered?

options.text: Server-render the public profiles; client-render the private dashboard
Client-render both, since every search engine runs JavaScript instantly
Server-render the dashboard; send profiles as an empty shell and script
Generate both as static PDF files each night, so no JavaScript is needed

questions.explanation: Public profiles need to be indexed and to load fast on slow phones, so sending ready HTML from the server suits them. The dashboard sits behind a login, is never indexed and is highly interactive, so client-side rendering fits it well.

why_others_wrong.b: Search engines can render JavaScript, but often later and less reliably, and slow phones still wait for the whole bundle before showing anything.
why_others_wrong.c: This is backwards: the private dashboard gains nothing from indexing, while the public profiles lose it.
why_others_wrong.d: Nightly PDFs cannot show live slot availability and are awkward to browse on a phone.

questions.key_justification: Render on the server where indexing and first-load speed matter; render on the client for logged-in, interactive views.

questions.prompt: Match each requirement to the technique that meets it.

items.text: A slot must never be sold to two students
Tutor profiles must appear in search results
A session must not be readable by injected scripts
Passwords must stay safe if the database leaks

targets.text: A slow, salted hash such as bcrypt or Argon2
A unique constraint on tutor and slot start

questions.explanation: The database constraint stops double booking, and server rendering gives crawlers ready HTML. The HttpOnly cookie hides the session from scripts, and a slow salted hash makes leaked password hashes expensive to crack.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Pairing password safety with the HttpOnly cookie: the cookie protects the session inside the browser, but only hashing protects passwords that are already sitting in a leaked database.

questions.key_justification: Each requirement is met by a control at a different layer: database, rendering, browser and storage.

import sys


def top_tutors(reviews, k, m):
    """reviews: list of (tutor_id, rating). Return up to k (tutor_id, average) pairs for tutors with at least m reviews, by average high to low, then more reviews first, then tutor id A to Z."""
    totals, counts = {}, {}
    for tutor, rating in reviews:
        totals[tutor] = totals.get(tutor, 0) + rating
        counts[tutor] = counts.get(tutor, 0) + 1
    rows = [(tutor, totals[tutor] / counts[tutor], counts[tutor]) for tutor in totals if counts[tutor] >= m]
    rows.sort(key=lambda r: (-r[1], -r[2], r[0]))
    return [(tutor, average) for tutor, average, _ in rows[:k]]


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    k, m = map(int, data[0].split())
    n = int(data[1])
    reviews = []
    for i in range(n):
        tutor, rating = data[2 + i].split()
        reviews.append((tutor, int(rating)))
    ranked = top_tutors(reviews, k, m)
    if not ranked:
        print("NONE")
    for tutor, average in ranked:
        print(tutor, format(average, ".2f"))


main()
code_pool.explanation: Accumulate a total and a count per tutor in dictionaries (the SQL equivalent is GROUP BY tutor with HAVING COUNT(*) >= m), then sort once with a composite key: negative average, negative count, then id. Sorting on the exact average, not the rounded one, keeps the order honest.
code_pool.key_justification: Group-by aggregation followed by a multi-key sort.

scenarios.title: Fixing the Slow, Glitchy MandiMitra App
scenarios.background: MandiMitra is a fictional app that shows farmers the daily vegetable prices at 50 wholesale markets around Saranpur. It has a React front end and an Express API on PostgreSQL. Last week the team moved the API to its own subdomain, and four problems appeared. Requests that work from curl now fail in the browser, with a console message saying the response has no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header. The market list page takes 4.2 seconds, and the API log shows one query for the 50 markets followed by 50 separate price queries, one per market. On the price chart page, the Network tab shows the same price request firing over and over. In the search box, typing 'tom' and then 'tomato' quickly sometimes leaves the results for 'tom' on screen.
constraints: Farmers check prices before 6 a.m., so fixes must ship this week
The API and the web app stay on separate subdomains
The team cannot add new infrastructure

questions.prompt: Requests succeed from curl, but the browser blocks them with the Access-Control-Allow-Origin message. What is the right fix?

options.text: Add an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header to the fetch request in React
Set fetch's mode to 'no-cors' so the browser stops blocking responses
Have the API allow the web app's origin in its CORS response headers
Ask farmers to install a browser extension that turns off CORS checks

questions.explanation: CORS is enforced by the browser using headers in the server's response, which is why curl, which does not enforce it, works while the browser does not. The API must name the web app's origin in Access-Control-Allow-Origin and answer preflight requests where they occur.

why_others_wrong.a: Access-Control-Allow-Origin is a response header; sending it from the client has no effect on the browser's check.
why_others_wrong.b: A no-cors request returns an opaque response whose body JavaScript cannot read, so the app still gets no prices.
why_others_wrong.d: Farmers cannot be asked to weaken their browser's security, and most would never do it.

questions.key_justification: CORS is fixed on the server by allowing the client's origin in the response headers.

questions.prompt: The market list runs one query for the markets and then one price query per market. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Run more API server instances behind a load balancer for the page
Fetch every market's prices in one query using a join or an IN list
Add an index on the market name column used to sort the list
Cache the list page in each browser for 24 hours with a header

questions.explanation: This is the N+1 query problem: 51 round trips to the database where one or two would do. Loading all prices in a single query, with a join or WHERE market_id IN (...), removes the per-market round trips, so load time no longer grows with the number of markets.

why_others_wrong.a: More servers do not reduce the 51 queries that each page load makes.
why_others_wrong.c: Sorting 50 markets is not the bottleneck; the cost is the 50 extra round trips, which an index does not remove.
why_others_wrong.d: Prices change daily, and a 24-hour browser cache would show farmers stale prices.

questions.key_justification: Fix N+1 queries by fetching related rows in one query, not by adding capacity.

questions.prompt: The price chart component contains this code: useEffect(() => { fetch(`/api/prices?market=${marketId}`).then(r => r.json()).then(setPrices); }); Why does the Network tab show the request repeating endlessly?

options.text: The effect has no dependency array, so every render runs it again
fetch() keeps retrying until the server sends back a cached response
React StrictMode repeats every effect in an endless loop in development
A silent JSON parse failure makes the browser resend the same request

questions.explanation: Without a dependency array, an effect runs after every render. setPrices stores a newly parsed array each time, which causes another render, which runs the effect again. Passing [marketId] as the dependency array makes it run only when the market changes.

why_others_wrong.b: fetch makes one request per call and has no automatic retries.
why_others_wrong.c: In development, StrictMode runs an effect one extra time on mount to expose bugs; it does not loop endlessly.
why_others_wrong.d: A failed JSON parse rejects the promise; the browser does not resend the request.

questions.key_justification: An effect with no dependency array runs after every render, so setting state inside it loops.

questions.prompt: Typing 'tom' and then 'tomato' quickly sometimes leaves the results for 'tom' on screen. Which two fixes make sure only the latest search's results are shown?

options.text: Abort the previous request with an AbortController when the input changes
Ignore any response whose search term no longer matches the current input
Add an index on the product name column so the queries finish faster
Raise the server's request timeout so slow responses are not dropped
Send the search as a POST request instead of a GET request with a query

questions.explanation: Two requests are in flight, and the slower one, for 'tom', can arrive last and overwrite the newer results. Aborting the old request or discarding responses for a stale term both guarantee that only the latest search updates the screen.

why_others_wrong.c: Faster queries make the race rarer but do not guarantee that responses arrive in order.
why_others_wrong.d: A longer timeout changes nothing about which response arrives last.
why_others_wrong.e: The HTTP method does not control the order in which responses arrive.

questions.key_justification: Out-of-order responses are fixed by cancelling or ignoring stale requests, not by making them faster.

questions.prompt: Match each symptom to its most likely cause.

items.text: Works from curl, but the browser reports a missing Access-Control-Allow-Origin header
Page load time grows in step with the number of markets listed
The Network tab shows the same GET request repeating many times a second
The results on screen sometimes belong to an older search term

targets.text: The API not allowing the web app's origin
An effect that runs after every render
One extra database query per market

questions.explanation: A browser-only failure naming Access-Control-Allow-Origin is a CORS setting on the API, and cost that grows per market is an N+1 query pattern. A request repeating on its own points to an effect that keeps re-running, while stale results point to responses finishing in the wrong order.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Matching the repeating request to out-of-order responses: a race involves two different requests finishing in the wrong order, while one request repeating on its own points to an effect that keeps re-running.

questions.key_justification: Each front-end or API bug has a distinct signature in the browser and the server logs.

code_pool.prompt: MandiMitra's search box sends a request on every keystroke, and responses can come back out of order. The first line is n, then n events in arrival order: `REQ id` when a request is sent (ids rise by one each time) and `RES id payload` when its response arrives. The screen should show a response only if its id is newer than the response already on screen, so a slow, older response never replaces a newer one. Complete `shown_after`. The program prints the payload on screen at the end (NONE if nothing was shown), then `ignored k`, the number of stale responses ignored.

def shown_after(events):
    """events: lists like ['REQ', '3'] or ['RES', '3', 'onion=31']. Return (payload on screen at the end or None, number of responses ignored as stale)."""

scenarios.title: Surviving the Diwali Rush at Yatrika Bus
scenarios.background: Yatrika is a fictional intercity bus-booking site serving 220 routes across the state of Vrindhar. It is a single Node.js application with one PostgreSQL database, built and run by four developers, and at peak it runs as several identical instances behind a load balancer. Normal traffic is about 30 requests per second; in Diwali week last year it reached 15 times that, and the site went down for two hours. Bus operators update schedules and fares once a day, while seat availability changes every few seconds. Customers pick a seat and then have up to 10 minutes to pay through a payment gateway that sometimes sends the same confirmation callback more than once. Operators also view a booking history table that now holds 4 million rows. Diwali is six weeks away.
constraints: Four developers and six weeks before the peak
A seat must never be sold twice
The payment gateway may repeat its confirmation callback
Several app instances run behind a load balancer at peak

questions.prompt: A developer proposes splitting the app into nine microservices before Diwali. What is the better plan for this team?

options.text: Split into nine services now, so each can scale on its own for Diwali
Keep the monolith, run more instances and fix the measured hot spots
Rewrite the app in a faster language before the six-week deadline
Move every table into separate databases owned by different teams

questions.explanation: Four developers cannot safely design, deploy and operate nine services in six weeks, and the split adds network calls and new failure modes right before the peak. The monolith already scales by adding instances behind the load balancer, and profiling shows which parts actually need work.

why_others_wrong.a: Microservices bring operational overhead and distributed failure modes that a four-person team cannot absorb in six weeks.
why_others_wrong.c: A rewrite in six weeks is high risk, and peak bottlenecks are more often in queries and the database than in the language.
why_others_wrong.d: There is only one team, and splitting the database breaks the transactions that keep seats from being sold twice.

questions.key_justification: Choose the architecture the team can operate; scale the existing system and fix measured bottlenecks first.

questions.prompt: Which caching plan fits Yatrika's data?

options.text: Cache seat availability for an hour, since it is read most often
Cache nothing at all, because any cache can show stale data
Cache full pages, seat maps included, at the CDN for a day
Cache route searches briefly; check seats live when booking

questions.explanation: Schedules and fares change once a day, so search results can be cached for a few minutes with little risk, removing most of the read load. Seat availability changes every few seconds, so the booking step must check it against the database, which stays the source of truth.

why_others_wrong.a: An hour-old seat map would show seats as free long after they were sold, causing failed bookings.
why_others_wrong.b: With no cache at all, the once-a-day search data hits the database on every request during a 15x peak.
why_others_wrong.c: A day-old seat map is badly wrong, and caching booking pages at a CDN can show one customer's data to another.

questions.key_justification: Cache data according to how often it changes; keep fast-changing, must-be-correct data live.

questions.prompt: The operators' booking history uses LIMIT 50 OFFSET n, newest first. Deep pages now take seconds and sometimes repeat rows as new bookings arrive. What is the best change?

options.text: Raise the page size to 500 rows so fewer pages need to be read
Send all 4 million rows once and paginate them in the browser
Use keyset pagination on created_at and id from the last row seen
Shuffle the rows randomly so each page load spreads the work evenly

questions.explanation: With OFFSET the database still reads and discards every skipped row, so deep pages get slower, and new inserts at the top shift rows onto the next page. Keyset pagination asks for rows older than the last seen (created_at, id), which an index on those columns serves directly, and new inserts do not shift later pages.

why_others_wrong.a: Bigger pages mean fewer pages, but deep offsets are still slow and rows still shift between pages.
why_others_wrong.b: Four million rows are far too much to send to a browser.
why_others_wrong.d: Random order makes the history useless and does nothing about the cost of OFFSET.

questions.key_justification: Keyset pagination stays fast at depth and stable under inserts; OFFSET does neither.

questions.prompt: Which measures prevent double bookings during the peak, whether from two customers or from repeated payment callbacks?

options.text: Hold the chosen seat in the database with a 10-minute expiry
Book inside a transaction that locks or uniquely constrains the seat row
Process payment callbacks idempotently, keyed by the gateway's payment id
Keep seat holds in each app instance's memory to avoid database writes
Check seat availability in the browser just before the payment page

questions.explanation: A hold in the database reserves the seat for every instance, and a transaction with a lock or unique constraint makes the final sale atomic. Idempotent callback handling means a repeated confirmation does not create a second booking.

why_others_wrong.d: Each instance has its own memory, so two instances could hold the same seat for two customers.
why_others_wrong.e: A browser-side check is stale by the time payment finishes and can be bypassed entirely.

questions.key_justification: Prevent double booking with shared state, atomic writes and idempotent handlers.

import sys


def charge_once(requests):
    """requests: list of (idempotency_key, amount) in arrival order. Charge each key only the first time it is seen. Return (total charged, number of repeated requests ignored)."""
    seen = set()
    charged = duplicates = 0
    for key, amount in requests:
        if key in seen:
            duplicates += 1
        else:
            seen.add(key)
            charged += amount
    return charged, duplicates


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    n = int(data[0])
    requests = []
    for i in range(n):
        key, amount = data[1 + i].split()
        requests.append((key, int(amount)))
    charged, duplicates = charge_once(requests)
    print("charged", charged)
    print("duplicates", duplicates)


main()

import sys


def simulate_lru(capacity, lookups):
    """Simulate a least-recently-used cache of the given capacity over the route lookups. Return (hits, misses, cache contents from most to least recently used)."""
    order = []          # most recently used last
    hits = misses = 0
    for route in lookups:
        if route in order:
            hits += 1
            order.remove(route)
        else:
            misses += 1
            if len(order) == capacity:
                order.pop(0)
        order.append(route)
    return hits, misses, list(reversed(order))


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    capacity, _ = map(int, data[0].split())
    lookups = data[1].split()
    hits, misses, cache = simulate_lru(capacity, lookups)
    print("hits", hits)
    print("misses", misses)
    print("cache", " ".join(cache) if cache else "EMPTY")


main()
code_pool.explanation: An LRU cache needs two things: a fast 'is it cached?' check and an order of recent use. A list works for small caches; the real structure is a hash map pointing into a doubly linked list (Python's OrderedDict), which makes both the lookup and the move-to-front O(1).
code_pool.key_justification: LRU = hash map for lookup + linked list for recency order.

scenarios.title: Shipping Kirana Khata to 5,000 Shops
scenarios.background: Kirana Khata is a fictional app from a startup in Devgarh that lets small grocery shops record credit sales and send customers payment reminders. It is a React progressive web app with a Node.js API and PostgreSQL, deployed as Docker images to several instances behind a load balancer using rolling deploys, so old and new versions serve traffic side by side for a few minutes. 5,000 shops start using it next month, many in towns where mobile data drops for minutes at a time. Shopkeepers pay a subscription through a payment gateway, and the API uses the gateway's secret key to create payment orders. Before launch, the team must rename the customers.phone column to mobile_number without downtime.
constraints: Shopkeepers must be able to record sales while offline
A bad release must be reversible within minutes
The payment gateway's secret key must never reach a shopkeeper's device

questions.prompt: Put these steps in order to rename customers.phone to mobile_number with no downtime during rolling deploys.

options.text: Add a nullable mobile_number column alongside phone
Deploy code that writes to both columns and still reads phone
With dual writes live, backfill mobile_number for the older rows
Deploy code that reads mobile_number while still writing both
Once no old version runs, stop writing phone and drop the column

questions.explanation: Adding the column first breaks nothing, and dual writes make sure new and edited rows get both values before the backfill copies the old ones. Reads switch only once every row is filled, and the old column is dropped only after no running version still uses it.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Backfilling before the dual-write code is deployed, so rows created or edited between the backfill and the deploy end up with an empty or stale mobile_number.

questions.key_justification: Expand, migrate, then contract: every step must work with both the old and the new code.

questions.prompt: The API needs the payment gateway's secret key to create payment orders. Where should the key live?

options.text: In the React build as an env variable such as VITE_PAYMENT_SECRET
In a config.json file committed to the repository for the whole team
On the server only, injected at runtime from a secret store or env
In the shopkeeper's localStorage after login, so it is fetched once

questions.explanation: A secret key must stay where only the team's own server code can read it. Loading it at runtime from a secret manager or the deployment's environment keeps it out of the repository, out of the images and off every device.

why_others_wrong.a: Variables built into a front-end bundle are embedded as plain text in the JavaScript that every visitor downloads.
why_others_wrong.b: Anything committed stays in the repository history and is exposed to everyone with access, now and in any future leak.
why_others_wrong.d: Sending the key to a device exposes it to anyone who inspects the browser.

questions.key_justification: Secret keys stay on the server and are injected at runtime, never built into client code or committed.

questions.prompt: Shopkeepers must record credit sales while their connection is down for minutes at a time. Which approach fits?

options.text: Hold unsent entries in React component state until the network returns
Save entries in IndexedDB and sync them later with client-generated ids
Retry each POST in a tight loop until the server finally accepts it
Store unsent entries in a cookie so they ride along on the next request

questions.explanation: IndexedDB persists in the browser across reloads and restarts, so entries survive until a connection returns and can be synced then. Ids generated on the device let the server recognise an entry it has already saved, so a retried sync does not create duplicates.

why_others_wrong.a: Component state is lost on a reload, a crash or when the phone closes the tab.
why_others_wrong.c: A tight retry loop drains the battery, and the entries are still lost if the app is closed.
why_others_wrong.d: Cookies hold only about 4 KB each and are sent with every request, so they cannot reliably queue a day's sales.

questions.key_justification: Offline-first means durable local storage plus idempotent sync.

questions.prompt: Which practices let the team roll back a bad release within minutes?

options.text: Deploy immutable, versioned images so the previous one can be redeployed
Keep each schema change compatible with the previous app version
Put risky features behind flags that can be switched off without a deploy
Rebuild the previous version from source on the build server when needed
Drop old columns in the same release that stops reading from them

questions.explanation: A versioned image can be redeployed in minutes, and a backward-compatible schema means the previous version still works against the current database. Feature flags turn off a risky change without any deploy at all.

why_others_wrong.d: Rebuilding under pressure is slow and may not reproduce the exact artefact that was running before.
why_others_wrong.e: If that release is rolled back, the old version expects a column that no longer exists and fails.

questions.key_justification: Fast rollback needs a ready artefact, a schema the old code can use, and switches that need no deploy.

questions.prompt: Match each practice to the failure it prevents.

items.text: Keeping secret keys on the server only
Building one image and promoting it through each stage

targets.text: Traffic keeps flowing to an instance that has stopped responding
Old instances crash mid-rollout because a column they use has vanished
A secret key is visible to anyone who opens the browser's developer tools
Production runs different code from the code that passed testing in staging

questions.explanation: Expand-and-contract keeps old instances working while the schema changes, and server-only secrets never reach a browser. Promoting one image guarantees that production runs exactly what was tested, and health checks take a dead instance out of rotation.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Matching health checks to the mid-rollout crash: health checks stop traffic reaching a failed instance, but only a compatible schema change keeps old instances from failing in the first place.

questions.key_justification: Each release practice protects against one distinct failure in deployment and operation.

code_pool.prompt: Kirana Khata works offline: a shopkeeper's actions are queued on the phone and replayed in order when the network returns. The first line is n, then n actions: `ADD name amount` (credit given), `PAY name amount` (money received) or `UNDO` (cancel the most recent action that has not already been undone; ignore it if there is none). Complete `replay`. The program prints `name balance` for every customer whose balance (credit minus payments) is not zero, sorted by name, or ALL CLEAR if every balance is zero.
code_pool.starter_code:
import sys


def replay(actions):
    """actions: ['ADD', name, amount], ['PAY', name, amount] or ['UNDO'], in the order they were made offline. UNDO cancels the most recent action not already undone (and does nothing if there is none). Return (name, balance) for every customer whose balance is not zero, sorted by name."""
    # Write your code here.
    return []


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    n = int(data[0])
    actions = [data[1 + i].split() for i in range(n)]
    balances = replay(actions)
    if not balances:
        print("ALL CLEAR")
    for name, amount in balances:
        print(name, amount)


main()
code_pool.explanation: Undo always cancels the most recent surviving action, which is exactly a stack: push each action, pop on UNDO. Replaying the stack afterwards into a dictionary of balances gives each customer's total. Order matters, which is why the offline queue must be replayed first in, first out.
code_pool.key_justification: Undo of the most recent action is a stack pop.

code_pool.reference_solution:
import heapq
import sys


def most_overdue(dues, today, k):
    """dues: list of (name, due_day, amount). A due is overdue when due_day < today. Return up to k (name, days_overdue, amount): most days overdue first, then larger amount, then name A to Z."""
    overdue = [(today - day, amount, name) for name, day, amount in dues if day < today]
    best = heapq.nsmallest(k, overdue, key=lambda x: (-x[0], -x[1], x[2]))
    return [(name, days, amount) for days, amount, name in best]


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    today, k = map(int, data[0].split())
    n = int(data[1])
    dues = []
    for i in range(n):
        name, day, amount = data[2 + i].split()
        dues.append((name, int(day), int(amount)))
    ranked = most_overdue(dues, today, k)
    if not ranked:
        print("NONE")
    for name, days, amount in ranked:
        print(name, days, amount)


main()
code_pool.explanation: Filter to overdue dues, then take the k best with a heap (heapq.nsmallest with a key of negative days, negative amount, name), which is O(n log k) instead of sorting everything. With small n a full sort is also correct; the heap matters when n is in the millions and k is small.
code_pool.key_justification: Top-k selection with a heap and a composite key.
